evidence.paraphrase: Śūrasena asks Indra for the detailed birth of the couple’s son after the vow. Indra says that through pleased Gaṇeśa’s favour the queen conceives and in the ninth month sees a son with two shoulders, beautiful face, nose and lotus eyes but no arms/hands, thighs/knees, lower legs or feet. She laments the gift, says remaining barren would have been better, questions removal of prior sin, the deity’s favour and Brahmin assurances, and repeatedly strikes her breast and forehead. The women weep; the king, ministers and townspeople hear and join the grief.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king questions Gaṇeśa’s compassion and declares his japa, tapas, remembrance, gifts, worship, Brahmin feeding, observance and homa apparently wasted. He says fate is stronger and effort fruitless, comparing the son with a mouse gained by breaking a mountain. Ministers urge him to cease grief because what must occur cannot be changed: they cite Rāma following the deer and Dharmarāja entering forbidden dice and then forest exile despite knowledge. Crying will not make the child beautiful; good unseen merit could allow his later improvement and kingship with time, as trees bear flowers and fruit. The king steadies himself and tells his wife to rise without grief. The king’s first verse is printed1 before the numbering resumes12; this span follows its sequential position.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king calls Brahmins, performs Gaṇeśa worship, svastivācana and auspicious śrāddha, and gives garlands, ornaments, clothes, cows and jewels. He gives clothes and appropriate gifts to friends, relatives, servants, musicians, bards, Cāraṇas and poor, blind and destitute people, distributing betel and sugar house to house. On the eleventh day he names the son Kārtavīrya and feeds the city with enthusiasm. Twelve years of the son’s life pass; Dattātreya voluntarily comes to his house.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king explicitly named Kṛtavīrya bows with his head at Dattātreya’s feet. The sage rises and embraces him. The king seats and honours him with seat, foot-water, arghya, a cow, clothes, sacred thread, incense, lamp, offerings, varied fruit, rubbing powder, betel, jewels, gold dakṣiṇā and foot-massage. When the sage is pleased and comfortably seated the king addresses him; the read-only fragment stops before the request.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Kṛtavīrya says many births’ merit now bears fruit in seeing Dattātreya and predicts future good from his favour, since wrongdoers do not see such sages. Dattātreya explicitly says he came to see the king’s extraordinary son. The king again laments his apparently fruitless practices and describes the son as a thorn in his heart. He brings the boy; the sage covers his eyes, then knows the relevant action through meditation. He predicts this very son will conquer all and diagnoses the king’s failure to perform ācamana after yawning during the Sankaṣṭa vigil as dishonouring the distress-removing vow. The son was born without limbs but can become complete through a remedy. The king accepts the diagnosis and asks what method will restore his son through the sage’s favour.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Compassionate Dattātreya teaches the CHILD the one-syllable mantra with its auxiliaries and prescribes devotional Gaṇeśa worship with it, fasting and one-meal rules. He predicts that after twelve years Gaṇeśa will give the child sight of himself and the deity’s mere glance will produce a divine body. Taking leave of the king, the sage disappears.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: After Dattātreya leaves, the footless son asks Kṛtavīrya to take him to a deep forest so he can practice for Gaṇeśa’s favour. Both parents weep at his request. The father sends him to a fine forest in a human-carried conveyance; servants place him in a leaf hut and return to the city. The boy remains there, firmly resolved on tapas.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The boy regularly japs the guru’s mantra, meditates Gaṇeśa with firm dedication, and lives on air without food like earth-clod or stone. Twelve years pass. Verse3 describes his condition with the printed nirvāṇam, retained without interpreting it as death or selecting another precise state. Pleased by his dedication and devotion, coral-formed Gaṇeśa rises from the pond and faces him. He notes the twelve years in the deserted forest frequented by lions and tigers and offers a boon according to the boy’s wish. Hearing him, the boy resumes bodily awareness.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The explicitly named son of Kṛtavīrya bows and speaks before many sages in vimānas. He requests continual nondeviating devotion to the deity’s feet, saying he has no enthusiasm to ask anything else. Nevertheless, to satisfy his parents, he also asks beauty of body pleasing to all.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Hearing the requests, māyā-bearing Gaṇeśa adopts aṇimā and enters the boy’s belly. With this entry Kṛtavīrya’s son gains a divine body with one thousand arms and two straight legs, standing like a mountain. Gods and divine sages shower flowers and praise both boy and deity with music. Kārtavīrya roars thunderously; the figure called Samavartin is greatly frightened and all earthly kings tremble, anticipating that he could shoot five hundred arrows in combat.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Brahmā and the other deities descend from their vimānas and give the boy varied boons. They say deities will regain lost objects through remembrance of him; he will remove the heart-resident ā maya of all worlds. They call him an actual Viṣṇu form with the name Sahasrārjuna, promise fame in three worlds for a kalpa, protection of good people and those taking refuge, victory over all enemies and sovereignty of the earth. The deity group then disappears.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: All kings bring elephants, horses, human conveyances, parasols, fly-whisks, lamps, chariots and other gifts. With Brahmins leading, Kārtavīrya installs a coral Gaṇeśa image in a great temple. Brahmins name it Pravālagaṇapa. He gives villages to the Brahmins appointed for its worship.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The place becomes famous as wish-accomplishing Pravāla-kṣetra. In a separate earlier account Śeṣa practices there desiring to bear earth and obtains many boons from Gaṇeśa: earth-bearing strength, omniscience, one thousand heads and supremacy among nine Nāga clans. With delighted mind he earlier installs the deity, bringing the second name Dharaṇīdhara, granting all wished fruits to those who remember or hear it.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Sahasrabāhu honours the Brahmins and takes leave of the kings, then returns to his city to see his mother and father. Both parents and the city rejoice at his restored form. His parents give varied gifts to eminent Brahmins.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Indra closes the Sankaṣṭa glory, saying it became known in the mortal world through Kṛtavīrya’s son and was experienced by gods and kings such as Candraseṇa. Remembrance alone gives accomplishment. Briefly, Rāvaṇa received the printed akhilājñatā and the Pāṇḍavas obtained their kingdom through its favour. Indra says his stalled vimāna will move to Amarāvatī if this vow’s merit is given into his hand. Brahmā says Śūrasena hears joyfully, bows to Indra, praises his own earlier merit for hearing such a vow and begins practicing. No merit transfer or actual departure occurs here.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: 73.3 prints nirvāṇaṃ tasya before the living child’s boon encounter; its precise condition is not normalized to death.73.31 prints akhilājñatā for Rāvaṇa’s brief vow-result; an exact English benefit is withheld.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct reread; transcription observed, unresolved interpretation not asserted.

evidence.paraphrase: Vyāsa asks Brahmā what Śūrasena did after hearing Indra. Brahmā says the king sends his messengers to bring a Sankaṣṭa practitioner. Searching house to house they find a fine vimāna and a severely diseased caṇḍālī with draining mouth, sores, insects, stench, wasted body and unclean appearance, whom Gaṇeśa’s messengers have come to take. Astonished, royal messengers bow to her and ask the divine servants who she was formerly, how she became like this and what merit accounts for her ascent.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Divine messengers identify her as daughter of the Bengal kṣatriya Śāraṅgadhara, called Sundarā/Sundarī in the verse. They praise her voice, face and beauty through comparisons with Rati and renowned nāyikās and describe men’s sexual agitation on seeing her. She pursues adulterous encounters, costly clothing, ornaments and sensual pleasures, openly known in Bengal like a prostitute, repeatedly deceiving her husband Citra and spending her father’s amassed wealth.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: One midnight she leaves her sleeping husband, dressed attractively; Citra catches her hand in anger and rebukes her habitual adultery.17 says her anger becomes quiet, then describes intoxication and strength from forbidden food. In darkness she takes a dagger in her right hand, cuts Citra’s belly and goes to the intended lover. An awake neighbour learns what happened and informs the king. Royal messengers wait, seize her on return, bring her to the king and execute her outside at his command. Yama’s messengers take her to terrible hell, where she suffers upside down, bitten by worms and recalling former deeds. At a kalpa’s end she is born an unfortunate caṇḍālī in the mortal world. The source prints5 for the verse in position15.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: In that rebirth she drinks liquor and sleeps during the day. Waking hungry in night’s first watch, she begs at a vow-practitioner’s home, receives food and eats at moonrise. By chance and of her own will she utters Gaṇeśa’s name; immediately Gaṇanātha sends the fine vimāna. The verse in position25 is printed5. Her conduct is not a deliberately undertaken proper vow.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Royal messengers recount their mission: Indra rode to see Gṛtsamāda, came to Bhṛśuṇḍi with gods, bowed and worshipped, received permission and worship, and headed home. In Śūrasena’s city his vehicle fell through the gaze of a leprous Vaiśya son. Indra told the king that Sankaṣṭa merit would restart it, prompting the search. They propose taking this woman to the king so she can transfer vow merit, afterward gain twice the merit and resume her ascent while Indra’s vehicle returns home. Gaṇeśa’s servants refuse, saying they have no order from him to give her to someone else.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The servants place her on the vimāna; she immediately gains divine radiance, clothing and ornaments and is taken toward Gaṇeśa amid divine music. The royal messengers return to Śūrasena and report. Her shining vehicle passes, her gaze falls on Indra’s craft, and contact with her craft’s air raises it while people and divine sages watch astonished. Indra actually goes to Amarāvatī and all return to their places; she, with divine body and freed from sin through Sankaṣṭa merit, reaches Vaināyaka’s abode. Properly hearing or carefully telling this story gives all desired objects and removes distress.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Having heard and seen the vow’s greatness, Śūrasena asks Vasiṣṭha for a suitable time to practice a vow giving immediate assurance. The sage prescribes Māgha dark fourth on Tuesday. The devoted king and unnamed wife assemble supplies. On that day he bathes, finishes daily rites, worships Gaṇeśa and honours Brahmins and Vasiṣṭha with permission. He concentrates on Gaṇeśa and japs the name, standing on one big toe until sunset. He bathes again, observes evening worship and starts proper pūjā with Vasiṣṭha.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The king prepares a great banana-pillared pavilion with clothing, ornaments, parasols, fly-whisks, mirrors, flowers, gems and lamps. A beautiful, well-proportioned gold Gaṇeśa image stands on a gold kalaśa. Amid Brahmin recitation, song, dance and instruments he performs Vedic and Purāṇic sixteen-service worship with pañcāmṛta, modaka/apūpa/laḍḍū/pāyasa and sugar, varied dishes, scented water, fruits, areca/betel, jewels and gold dakṣiṇā, dūrvā, light and mantra-flowers. He gives arghya to tithi, Gaṇeśa and Moon, honours and feeds Brahmins and gives ten thousand cows, clothes, ornaments and fees. He eats with friends and kin and keeps night vigil with song, instruments and stories. At dawn he bathes and worships again, then gives the image, furnishings and dakṣiṇā to Vasiṣṭha. Pleased, Gaṇeśa sends a prosperous vimāna.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The messengers place the king, bearing Gaṇeśa’s form, aboard while people rejoice. They say pleased Vināyaka sent them, eager to see him. The king weeps with joy and says the unfathomable, unmanifest Lord beyond speech and mind, praised by Vedas, śāstras and deities, has no need to see him; his being remembered is great fortune. The messengers admit devotees make the formless deity assume form. The king expresses a great wish: how can he leave his city for Gaṇeśa when he has not even consumed Hālāhala apart from its people? He cannot enjoy highest happiness without them. They agree his wish should be fulfilled, fearing Gaṇeśa’s anger if they refuse.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The messengers immediately put all the city’s beings aboard, explicitly all caturākaraja creatures, with divine clothes and ornaments. Some wonder how they gained this without their own merit; others attribute rescue to the king’s merit, comparing metal becoming gold through a treasure and sinners attaining perfection through saintly speech. The attendants attempt upward movement, but the craft remains inert on earth. Some spot a leprous man and urge discarding him, saying the craft will rise when he descends. Śūrasena instead offers to exclude himself and carry all others, or asks the man’s former birth, sin and a compassionate remedy. The messengers reassure him and undertake to explain. Numbering prints15 at position35 and4 at41.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The messengers describe a learned ascetic Brahmin devoted to gods and Brahmins in Gauḍa city. His son’s mother is Śākinī; the son’s faithful wife is Sāvitrī. An only-child affection leads to adornments, great beauty compared with Rati’s husband, and parents unwilling to endure separation. In youth he abandons his wife for adultery, slander and disregard for paternal counsel. When an unnamed captivating prostitute comes, he puts away his ornaments before his parents, then steals them and gives them to her. He lives absorbed in her amid scents and pleasures, compared in dedication with a Brahman-focused yogin.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The distressed father searches every house for his son without eating or drinking, but cannot see him. At midnight he tells his wife their home is empty without Budha and asks when life-preserving sight will return. Śākinī says hunger, thirst, anxiety and grief exhaust her and only seeing the boy will sustain her. Dūrva takes his staff and searches again. An elderly man of lowest caste named Bhīma tells him Budha is playing in the prostitute’s home, passion-bound and disregarding parentage, and says his grief is wasted. Dūrva asks how his son could become absorbed there and goes to that house.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The father seizes the intoxicated, red-eyed son’s hand and rebukes him, preferring a thorn-tree or stone to such a son and questioning his life. Budha strikes the father’s face, insults him for obstructing his pleasure and kicks him to death.24 reports Hareśvara with so’vadat at the father’s death; its speaker is not assigned without support. The son rejoices, binds the father’s foot, throws the body away, drinks and returns to the prostitute. Next morning Śākinī joyfully embraces him, with milk flowing through affection, asks where he was, says both parents waited without food/water, and repeatedly urges him to find his searching father. Angered, he hits her head with dry wood, knows her unconscious, ties and throws her outside and returns to the prostitute. Good people cremate both parents with their wood. The king does not punish him because he is a Brahmin.21 is printed2.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: When Budha returns, wife Sāvitrī gently urges virtuous conduct suited to his respected birth: act now for future-world happiness, in youth for old age, during eight months for the rains and by day for the night. She says the king excuses him through affection for his father and his Brahmin status, asks why he abandoned his faithful, beautiful and compliant lawful wife for a prostitute, and describes public condemnation, fear of speaking to him and her shame. She proposes marital companionship rather than public wrongdoing, urges him to leave the prostitute and abandon ignorant or negligent deeds, and says continuing otherwise loses both this world and the next. Her words pierce Budha deeply.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Enraged, Budha insults Sāvitrī and threatens her with his parents’ fate. She says one who did not respect his educating parents cannot protect her, and regards death at her husband’s hand as better for a virtuous wife. He seizes her hair and beats her with wood, clods, fists and stones. Through prior merit she remembers Rāma in husband-form and dies from his blows to vital parts. She goes to heaven with divine body and enjoys highest happiness. He drags her by the foot and throws her far away at night, then tells the prostitute he destroyed everyone for her and resumes pleasure.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: After much time Budha visits sage Kalabha’s house while the sage bathes, seizes his beautiful wife by the hair, embraces, kisses and rapes her. Sulabhā says her parents’ given name has made her easy to him, condemns the assault in her husband’s absence and curses him to become a leper in another birth whose very name people will avoid. He flees frightened to the prostitute but resumes drink and pleasure. Brahmā declines further wrongdoings, saying telling others’ faults diminishes merit. Budha eventually dies; Yama orders messengers to throw him into hell until the elemental dissolution. Having endured that, he is born in a Vaiśya home, severely leprous through the sage’s wife’s curse. The discourse condemns his deeds, prescribes clothed bathing after touching him and avoidance of his name, and says removing him will raise the craft.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Hearing the messengers’ account, Śūrasena trembles, says he did not know these acts, rises and bows anxiously. He asks compassionately for a way to remove all the wrongdoer’s defects. They tell him to rise and listen: Gaṇeśa has a famous FOUR-syllable name; japa it into the man’s ear and all faults will cease like darkness at sunrise. They say he is not qualified for other remedies, so the name alone should be japped.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: At the messengers’ direction Śūrasena japs the four-syllable name into the Vaiśya’s ear THREE times, with jayapūrvam prefix wording retained. Merely hearing Gajānana, the man gains a divine body shining like the dawn sun. All sin ends through hearing the name alone; he boards the craft. By Vighnarāja’s command, the messengers immediately bring that vehicle with all its beings to Vaināyaka’s abode. Brahmā closes the answers and praises Sankaṣṭa-caturthī as righteous, fame- and life-giving, granting accomplishment by hearing, quelling suffering and obstacles, and the power of dūrvā and the name.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: The father has given up life;24 reports hareśvareti so’vadat, followed by rejoicing son. The exact utterance speaker is not securely selected; no chanting act is assigned to a dead father or to Budha without clarification.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct reread; transcription observed, unresolved interpretation not asserted.

assertions.value: Grief cannot restore beauty; if unseen merit is favourable the boy may later improve and become king72.16–20. Rāma/deer and Dharmarāja/dice are brief examples, not full retellings.
Kārtavīrya on eleventh day72.25; actual son’s explicit name does not silently emend earlier68.3/71.19 performer names.
Dattātreya diagnoses omitted ācamana after yawning during Sankaṣṭa-vow vigil72.38 as causing the limb-deficient birth; king accepts and asks remedy39.
A method through the sage’s favour by which his son becomes complete in limbs72.39.
Divine body, one thousand arms and two straight legs73.10–12.
The Brahmā-led group calls him an actual Viṣṇu form73.17; source boon speech attribution.
They propose Sundarī transfer vow merit to restart Indra’s vehicle and receive doubled merit afterward74.33–36; the divine messengers refuse37, so no actual gift is asserted.
Take the city’s beings with him; he cannot enjoy supreme happiness without them75.31–32. Hālāhala wording is his stated solidarity comparison, not a separately narrated poisoning episode.
All caturākaraja creatures, not only humans75.34.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: The queen conceives through the pleased deity’s favour and bears the described child in the ninth month.
boons_and_powers.notes: Actual narrative favour, not a new boon invitation/request/grant scene. Her lament questions efficacy; it is not narrator proof that all prior merit was absent.

boons_and_powers.granted: One-syllable mantra with auxiliaries is taught to the child.
boons_and_powers.mechanism: Prescribed fasting/one-meal worship; predicts Gaṇeśa appearance after twelve years and divine body through his mere glance.
boons_and_powers.notes: The glance is a guru’s future prediction, not the subsequently narrated actual transformation mechanism. Twelve years describes required practice/predicted appearance, not the boon’s lasting duration. Actual73.10–12 uses aṇimā entry rather than explicitly enacting the predicted glance.

boons_and_powers.motive: Please his parents through bodily beauty.
boons_and_powers.requested: Continual nondeviating devotion; additionally bodily beauty pleasing to all for his parents’ happiness.
boons_and_powers.granted: Actual divine body with one thousand arms and two straight legs.
boons_and_powers.mechanism: Gaṇeśa adopts aṇimā and enters the boy’s belly.
boons_and_powers.notes: Personal boon invitation and requests. Subsequent physical response will be separately evidenced; no explicit verbal assent to the devotion request is supplied.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: Kings anticipate his capacity to release five hundred arrows in combat.
boons_and_powers.notes: Anticipated capacity73.15, not a narrated volley or invented weapon-counter sequence.

boons_and_powers.granted: Deities’ recovery of lost objects through remembrance of him; removal of all worlds’ heart-resident ā maya; Viṣṇu-form/Sahasrārjuna designation; three-world fame for a kalpa; good/refugee protection; victory over all enemies and earth sovereignty.
boons_and_powers.duration: A kalpa qualifies his three-world fame73.18.
boons_and_powers.notes: No exact request to this deity group is narrated. Āmaya is retained as heart-resident affliction, not a specific modern cardiac diagnosis. Remembrance/lost objects is not broadened beyond the verse’s deity wording.

boons_and_powers.granted: Earth-bearing capacity, omniscience, one thousand heads, supremacy among nine Nāga clans.
boons_and_powers.notes: Motive explicitly stated; the wording of a personal request is not given. Chronology is an embedded earlier practice/installation.

boons_and_powers.trigger: Remember or hear the Dharaṇīdhara name/account73.26.
boons_and_powers.notes: The precise formula speaks of remembering/hearing, without inventing a visit or separate practice requirement.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: Accomplishment even through remembering the vow73.30.
boons_and_powers.notes: Null means unstated in examined passage, not independently proven absent from whole work. Reported efficacy is a POWER unless an explicit personal boon is narrated.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: Reported earlier attainment of their kingdom through the vow’s favour.
boons_and_powers.notes: Only the brief reported result73.31 is extracted; no epic battle or genealogy is added.
The source’s terse efficacy claim is retained raw; no silent omniscience or other translated benefit.

boons_and_powers.austerity_or_circumstances: Drinks and sleeps by day; begs and eats the practitioner’s food at moonrise; voluntarily utters Gaṇeśa by chance.
boons_and_powers.mechanism: Gaṇeśa actually sends the rescue vimāna after the narrated moonrise meal and name utterance.
boons_and_powers.notes: An unintended vow-like sequence; not a knowingly completed proper vow or a formal personal boon request.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: Actual divine body and attainment of Vaināyaka’s abode, free from sin through Sankaṣṭa merit.
boons_and_powers.notes: The rescue has an actual ending; the text does not state she performed all prescribed vow services consciously.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: His stalled vehicle rises after her gaze falls on it and her vehicle’s air touches it; he actually reaches Amarāvatī.
boons_and_powers.notes: No accepted voluntary transfer or doubled merit is narrated. Both gaze and contact with the passing vehicle’s air are preserved.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: All desired objects and removal of distress.
boons_and_powers.trigger: Proper hearing or careful telling of this account.
boons_and_powers.notes: Null means unstated in examined passage, not independently proven absent from whole work. Reported efficacy is a POWER unless an explicit personal boon is narrated.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: The pleased deity sends a prosperous rescue vimāna after the king’s actual observance and final image-gift.
boons_and_powers.trigger: The described proper vow and completion worship/gift.
boons_and_powers.notes: Not yet an arrival at the final abode; collective boarding and the new obstruction follow.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: After being killed she actually goes to heaven in divine body and enjoys highest happiness.
boons_and_powers.notes: Her Rāma remembrance is attributed to prior merit; chronology alone is not promoted to a new personal boon or an explicit sole causal trigger.

boons_and_powers.granted: Curse: leprosy in another birth and avoidance of his name.
boons_and_powers.trigger: His rape of Sulabhā during Kalabha’s absence.
boons_and_powers.duration: The curse targets another birth; no fixed year-count.
boons_and_powers.counter: Name-hearing gives divine body and all-sin removal before collective transport76.69–72.
boons_and_powers.notes: A curse, not favourable personal boon. Actual later Vaiśya-leper birth is narrated59; dissolution qualifies the preceding hell stay58, not silently the curse duration.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: Hearing Gajānana from the king gives a divine body and ends all sin; he boards and reaches the abode with everyone.
boons_and_powers.trigger: The king’s three utterances into his ear of the four-syllable name.
boons_and_powers.restrictions: The messengers say other remedies are not authorized for him76.68.
boons_and_powers.notes: Jayapūrvam69 is preserved as prefix wording; no new five-syllable mantra is invented.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: The entire boarded city’s beings reach Vaināyaka’s abode by Vighnarāja’s command.
boons_and_powers.notes: Actual collective transport, not merely the75.33 promise or failed75.39 lift.

boons_and_powers.mechanism: Righteousness, fame, life benefit, all accomplishments, suffering and obstacle relief as praised in the closing account.
boons_and_powers.notes: Null means unstated in examined passage, not independently proven absent from whole work. Reported efficacy is a POWER unless an explicit personal boon is narrated.

narrative_events.details: Śūrasena asks Indra for the detailed birth of the couple’s son after the vow. Indra says that through pleased Gaṇeśa’s favour the queen conceives and in the ninth month sees a son with two shoulders, beautiful face, nose and lotus eyes but no arms/hands, thighs/knees, lower legs or feet. She laments the gift, says remaining barren would have been better, questions removal of prior sin, the deity’s favour and Brahmin assurances, and repeatedly strikes her breast and forehead. The women weep; the king, ministers and townspeople hear and join the grief.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual sonbirth and the detailed absence of limbs are narrated before the remedy; no normal-limbed birth is substituted.

narrative_events.details: The king questions Gaṇeśa’s compassion and declares his japa, tapas, remembrance, gifts, worship, Brahmin feeding, observance and homa apparently wasted. He says fate is stronger and effort fruitless, comparing the son with a mouse gained by breaking a mountain. Ministers urge him to cease grief because what must occur cannot be changed: they cite Rāma following the deer and Dharmarāja entering forbidden dice and then forest exile despite knowledge. Crying will not make the child beautiful; good unseen merit could allow his later improvement and kingship with time, as trees bear flowers and fruit. The king steadies himself and tells his wife to rise without grief. The king’s first verse is printed1 before the numbering resumes12; this span follows its sequential position.
narrative_events.outcome: Attributed fatalist complaint is answered by ministerial counsel and an explicitly prospective possible improvement.

narrative_events.details: The king calls Brahmins, performs Gaṇeśa worship, svastivācana and auspicious śrāddha, and gives garlands, ornaments, clothes, cows and jewels. He gives clothes and appropriate gifts to friends, relatives, servants, musicians, bards, Cāraṇas and poor, blind and destitute people, distributing betel and sugar house to house. On the eleventh day he names the son Kārtavīrya and feeds the city with enthusiasm. Twelve years of the son’s life pass; Dattātreya voluntarily comes to his house.
narrative_events.outcome: The boy receives an explicit name on day11 and reaches age12 before the voluntary sage visit.

narrative_events.details: The king explicitly named Kṛtavīrya bows with his head at Dattātreya’s feet. The sage rises and embraces him. The king seats and honours him with seat, foot-water, arghya, a cow, clothes, sacred thread, incense, lamp, offerings, varied fruit, rubbing powder, betel, jewels, gold dakṣiṇā and foot-massage. When the sage is pleased and comfortably seated the king addresses him; the read-only fragment stops before the request.
narrative_events.outcome: The visitor is welcomed before the exact request and explanation; the next primary unread verse is31.

narrative_events.details: Kṛtavīrya says many births’ merit now bears fruit in seeing Dattātreya and predicts future good from his favour, since wrongdoers do not see such sages. Dattātreya explicitly says he came to see the king’s extraordinary son. The king again laments his apparently fruitless practices and describes the son as a thorn in his heart. He brings the boy; the sage covers his eyes, then knows the relevant action through meditation. He predicts this very son will conquer all and diagnoses the king’s failure to perform ācamana after yawning during the Sankaṣṭa vigil as dishonouring the distress-removing vow. The son was born without limbs but can become complete through a remedy. The king accepts the diagnosis and asks what method will restore his son through the sage’s favour.
narrative_events.outcome: Meditative diagnosis identifies one exact ritual omission; the father asks a remedy, without a new unnamed sin being invented.

narrative_events.details: Compassionate Dattātreya teaches the CHILD the one-syllable mantra with its auxiliaries and prescribes devotional Gaṇeśa worship with it, fasting and one-meal rules. He predicts that after twelve years Gaṇeśa will give the child sight of himself and the deity’s mere glance will produce a divine body. Taking leave of the king, the sage disappears.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual guru instruction is distinguished from the future appearance-and-glance prediction.

narrative_events.details: After Dattātreya leaves, the footless son asks Kṛtavīrya to take him to a deep forest so he can practice for Gaṇeśa’s favour. Both parents weep at his request. The father sends him to a fine forest in a human-carried conveyance; servants place him in a leaf hut and return to the city. The boy remains there, firmly resolved on tapas.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual relocation with servants and a leaf hut prepares the child’s separate twelve-year practice.

narrative_events.details: The boy regularly japs the guru’s mantra, meditates Gaṇeśa with firm dedication, and lives on air without food like earth-clod or stone. Twelve years pass. Verse3 describes his condition with the printed nirvāṇam, retained without interpreting it as death or selecting another precise state. Pleased by his dedication and devotion, coral-formed Gaṇeśa rises from the pond and faces him. He notes the twelve years in the deserted forest frequented by lions and tigers and offers a boon according to the boy’s wish. Hearing him, the boy resumes bodily awareness.
narrative_events.outcome: Twelve-year air-fed practice leads to an actual coral-form appearance and boon invitation; the exact nirvāṇam condition remains under review.

narrative_events.details: The explicitly named son of Kṛtavīrya bows and speaks before many sages in vimānas. He requests continual nondeviating devotion to the deity’s feet, saying he has no enthusiasm to ask anything else. Nevertheless, to satisfy his parents, he also asks beauty of body pleasing to all.
narrative_events.outcome: The two requested benefits and the parents’ happiness motive are explicit; no demand for a thousand arms is put in the child’s mouth.

narrative_events.details: Hearing the requests, māyā-bearing Gaṇeśa adopts aṇimā and enters the boy’s belly. With this entry Kṛtavīrya’s son gains a divine body with one thousand arms and two straight legs, standing like a mountain. Gods and divine sages shower flowers and praise both boy and deity with music. Kārtavīrya roars thunderously; the figure called Samavartin is greatly frightened and all earthly kings tremble, anticipating that he could shoot five hundred arrows in combat.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual aṇimā entry restores a divine thousand-armed/two-legged body. Five hundred combat arrows are an anticipated capacity, not an enacted battle.

narrative_events.details: Brahmā and the other deities descend from their vimānas and give the boy varied boons. They say deities will regain lost objects through remembrance of him; he will remove the heart-resident ā maya of all worlds. They call him an actual Viṣṇu form with the name Sahasrārjuna, promise fame in three worlds for a kalpa, protection of good people and those taking refuge, victory over all enemies and sovereignty of the earth. The deity group then disappears.
narrative_events.outcome: These later grants have a collective divine grantor; they are separated from Gaṇeśa’s earlier physical response.

narrative_events.details: All kings bring elephants, horses, human conveyances, parasols, fly-whisks, lamps, chariots and other gifts. With Brahmins leading, Kārtavīrya installs a coral Gaṇeśa image in a great temple. Brahmins name it Pravālagaṇapa. He gives villages to the Brahmins appointed for its worship.
narrative_events.outcome: An actual installed coral image and endowed worship establish the site after the transformation.

narrative_events.details: The place becomes famous as wish-accomplishing Pravāla-kṣetra. In a separate earlier account Śeṣa practices there desiring to bear earth and obtains many boons from Gaṇeśa: earth-bearing strength, omniscience, one thousand heads and supremacy among nine Nāga clans. With delighted mind he earlier installs the deity, bringing the second name Dharaṇīdhara, granting all wished fruits to those who remember or hear it.
narrative_events.outcome: A source flashback explains the second site-name; Śeṣa’s boons are not assigned to Kārtavīrya.

narrative_events.details: Sahasrabāhu honours the Brahmins and takes leave of the kings, then returns to his city to see his mother and father. Both parents and the city rejoice at his restored form. His parents give varied gifts to eminent Brahmins.
narrative_events.outcome: The son actually returns to both parents and receives their joy; the birth/remedy/reunion sequence has a bounded ending.

narrative_events.details: Indra closes the Sankaṣṭa glory, saying it became known in the mortal world through Kṛtavīrya’s son and was experienced by gods and kings such as Candraseṇa. Remembrance alone gives accomplishment. Briefly, Rāvaṇa received the printed akhilājñatā and the Pāṇḍavas obtained their kingdom through its favour. Indra says his stalled vimāna will move to Amarāvatī if this vow’s merit is given into his hand. Brahmā says Śūrasena hears joyfully, bows to Indra, praises his own earlier merit for hearing such a vow and begins practicing. No merit transfer or actual departure occurs here.
narrative_events.outcome: The exemplum returns to the stalled-vimāna frame with a conditional merit request; Śūrasena starts a vow, while the vehicle remains unresolved.

narrative_events.details: Vyāsa asks Brahmā what Śūrasena did after hearing Indra. Brahmā says the king sends his messengers to bring a Sankaṣṭa practitioner. Searching house to house they find a fine vimāna and a severely diseased caṇḍālī with draining mouth, sores, insects, stench, wasted body and unclean appearance, whom Gaṇeśa’s messengers have come to take. Astonished, royal messengers bow to her and ask the divine servants who she was formerly, how she became like this and what merit accounts for her ascent.
narrative_events.outcome: The royal search encounters a rescue already ordered by Gaṇeśa and elicits a past-life account.

narrative_events.details: Divine messengers identify her as daughter of the Bengal kṣatriya Śāraṅgadhara, called Sundarā/Sundarī in the verse. They praise her voice, face and beauty through comparisons with Rati and renowned nāyikās and describe men’s sexual agitation on seeing her. She pursues adulterous encounters, costly clothing, ornaments and sensual pleasures, openly known in Bengal like a prostitute, repeatedly deceiving her husband Citra and spending her father’s amassed wealth.
narrative_events.outcome: Her father and husband are distinct named men; beauty comparisons do not establish identity with Rati or another woman.

narrative_events.details: One midnight she leaves her sleeping husband, dressed attractively; Citra catches her hand in anger and rebukes her habitual adultery.17 says her anger becomes quiet, then describes intoxication and strength from forbidden food. In darkness she takes a dagger in her right hand, cuts Citra’s belly and goes to the intended lover. An awake neighbour learns what happened and informs the king. Royal messengers wait, seize her on return, bring her to the king and execute her outside at his command. Yama’s messengers take her to terrible hell, where she suffers upside down, bitten by worms and recalling former deeds. At a kalpa’s end she is born an unfortunate caṇḍālī in the mortal world. The source prints5 for the verse in position15.
narrative_events.outcome: Husband-killing, report, royal execution, hell suffering and kalpa-end rebirth are narrated in order.

narrative_events.details: In that rebirth she drinks liquor and sleeps during the day. Waking hungry in night’s first watch, she begs at a vow-practitioner’s home, receives food and eats at moonrise. By chance and of her own will she utters Gaṇeśa’s name; immediately Gaṇanātha sends the fine vimāna. The verse in position25 is printed5. Her conduct is not a deliberately undertaken proper vow.
narrative_events.outcome: Daytime drunken sleep, moonrise food and voluntary name utterance precede actual divine rescue, without a fabricated conscious complete observance.

narrative_events.details: Royal messengers recount their mission: Indra rode to see Gṛtsamāda, came to Bhṛśuṇḍi with gods, bowed and worshipped, received permission and worship, and headed home. In Śūrasena’s city his vehicle fell through the gaze of a leprous Vaiśya son. Indra told the king that Sankaṣṭa merit would restart it, prompting the search. They propose taking this woman to the king so she can transfer vow merit, afterward gain twice the merit and resume her ascent while Indra’s vehicle returns home. Gaṇeśa’s servants refuse, saying they have no order from him to give her to someone else.
narrative_events.outcome: Merit transfer and doubling are only a royal-emissary proposal; divine messengers refuse without Gaṇeśa’s authorization.

narrative_events.details: The servants place her on the vimāna; she immediately gains divine radiance, clothing and ornaments and is taken toward Gaṇeśa amid divine music. The royal messengers return to Śūrasena and report. Her shining vehicle passes, her gaze falls on Indra’s craft, and contact with her craft’s air raises it while people and divine sages watch astonished. Indra actually goes to Amarāvatī and all return to their places; she, with divine body and freed from sin through Sankaṣṭa merit, reaches Vaināyaka’s abode. Properly hearing or carefully telling this story gives all desired objects and removes distress.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual divine-body rescue and abode, plus gaze/vehicle-air contact restarting Indra’s craft, occur without the rejected merit-transfer transaction.

narrative_events.details: Having heard and seen the vow’s greatness, Śūrasena asks Vasiṣṭha for a suitable time to practice a vow giving immediate assurance. The sage prescribes Māgha dark fourth on Tuesday. The devoted king and unnamed wife assemble supplies. On that day he bathes, finishes daily rites, worships Gaṇeśa and honours Brahmins and Vasiṣṭha with permission. He concentrates on Gaṇeśa and japs the name, standing on one big toe until sunset. He bathes again, observes evening worship and starts proper pūjā with Vasiṣṭha.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual timed observance and guru-guided services follow the earlier exemplary rescue.

narrative_events.details: The king prepares a great banana-pillared pavilion with clothing, ornaments, parasols, fly-whisks, mirrors, flowers, gems and lamps. A beautiful, well-proportioned gold Gaṇeśa image stands on a gold kalaśa. Amid Brahmin recitation, song, dance and instruments he performs Vedic and Purāṇic sixteen-service worship with pañcāmṛta, modaka/apūpa/laḍḍū/pāyasa and sugar, varied dishes, scented water, fruits, areca/betel, jewels and gold dakṣiṇā, dūrvā, light and mantra-flowers. He gives arghya to tithi, Gaṇeśa and Moon, honours and feeds Brahmins and gives ten thousand cows, clothes, ornaments and fees. He eats with friends and kin and keeps night vigil with song, instruments and stories. At dawn he bathes and worships again, then gives the image, furnishings and dakṣiṇā to Vasiṣṭha. Pleased, Gaṇeśa sends a prosperous vimāna.
narrative_events.outcome: Complete actual ritual and donations precede the deity’s sent vehicle; the exact ten-thousand-cow gift is retained.

narrative_events.details: The messengers place the king, bearing Gaṇeśa’s form, aboard while people rejoice. They say pleased Vināyaka sent them, eager to see him. The king weeps with joy and says the unfathomable, unmanifest Lord beyond speech and mind, praised by Vedas, śāstras and deities, has no need to see him; his being remembered is great fortune. The messengers admit devotees make the formless deity assume form. The king expresses a great wish: how can he leave his city for Gaṇeśa when he has not even consumed Hālāhala apart from its people? He cannot enjoy highest happiness without them. They agree his wish should be fulfilled, fearing Gaṇeśa’s anger if they refuse.
narrative_events.outcome: The king requests collective inclusion; messengers promise accommodation before the later actual lift attempt.

narrative_events.details: The messengers immediately put all the city’s beings aboard, explicitly all caturākaraja creatures, with divine clothes and ornaments. Some wonder how they gained this without their own merit; others attribute rescue to the king’s merit, comparing metal becoming gold through a treasure and sinners attaining perfection through saintly speech. The attendants attempt upward movement, but the craft remains inert on earth. Some spot a leprous man and urge discarding him, saying the craft will rise when he descends. Śūrasena instead offers to exclude himself and carry all others, or asks the man’s former birth, sin and a compassionate remedy. The messengers reassure him and undertake to explain. Numbering prints15 at position35 and4 at41.
narrative_events.outcome: All classes are accommodated, but lift actually fails. The king refuses the proposed abandonment and explicitly seeks remedy or his own exclusion.

narrative_events.details: The messengers describe a learned ascetic Brahmin devoted to gods and Brahmins in Gauḍa city. His son’s mother is Śākinī; the son’s faithful wife is Sāvitrī. An only-child affection leads to adornments, great beauty compared with Rati’s husband, and parents unwilling to endure separation. In youth he abandons his wife for adultery, slander and disregard for paternal counsel. When an unnamed captivating prostitute comes, he puts away his ornaments before his parents, then steals them and gives them to her. He lives absorbed in her amid scents and pleasures, compared in dedication with a Brahman-focused yogin.
narrative_events.outcome: The source introduces distinct mother and wife before the son’s abandonment and theft; the unnamed prostitute is not merged with Sundarī74.

narrative_events.details: The distressed father searches every house for his son without eating or drinking, but cannot see him. At midnight he tells his wife their home is empty without Budha and asks when life-preserving sight will return. Śākinī says hunger, thirst, anxiety and grief exhaust her and only seeing the boy will sustain her. Dūrva takes his staff and searches again. An elderly man of lowest caste named Bhīma tells him Budha is playing in the prostitute’s home, passion-bound and disregarding parentage, and says his grief is wasted. Dūrva asks how his son could become absorbed there and goes to that house.
narrative_events.outcome: Source explicitly names the father Dūrva and son Budha and gives Bhīma’s information; no Pāṇḍava or planetary identity is inferred.

narrative_events.details: The father seizes the intoxicated, red-eyed son’s hand and rebukes him, preferring a thorn-tree or stone to such a son and questioning his life. Budha strikes the father’s face, insults him for obstructing his pleasure and kicks him to death.24 reports Hareśvara with so’vadat at the father’s death; its speaker is not assigned without support. The son rejoices, binds the father’s foot, throws the body away, drinks and returns to the prostitute. Next morning Śākinī joyfully embraces him, with milk flowing through affection, asks where he was, says both parents waited without food/water, and repeatedly urges him to find his searching father. Angered, he hits her head with dry wood, knows her unconscious, ties and throws her outside and returns to the prostitute. Good people cremate both parents with their wood. The king does not punish him because he is a Brahmin.21 is printed2.
narrative_events.outcome: Both parents are killed and cremated, and royal nonpunishment is explicitly explained. The single death-utterance speaker remains unresolved.

narrative_events.details: When Budha returns, wife Sāvitrī gently urges virtuous conduct suited to his respected birth: act now for future-world happiness, in youth for old age, during eight months for the rains and by day for the night. She says the king excuses him through affection for his father and his Brahmin status, asks why he abandoned his faithful, beautiful and compliant lawful wife for a prostitute, and describes public condemnation, fear of speaking to him and her shame. She proposes marital companionship rather than public wrongdoing, urges him to leave the prostitute and abandon ignorant or negligent deeds, and says continuing otherwise loses both this world and the next. Her words pierce Budha deeply.
narrative_events.outcome: A detailed wife-to-husband corrective conversation precedes his threat and her death; no new woman or mother identity is substituted.

narrative_events.details: Enraged, Budha insults Sāvitrī and threatens her with his parents’ fate. She says one who did not respect his educating parents cannot protect her, and regards death at her husband’s hand as better for a virtuous wife. He seizes her hair and beats her with wood, clods, fists and stones. Through prior merit she remembers Rāma in husband-form and dies from his blows to vital parts. She goes to heaven with divine body and enjoys highest happiness. He drags her by the foot and throws her far away at night, then tells the prostitute he destroyed everyone for her and resumes pleasure.
narrative_events.outcome: Wife-killing and her actual heavenly/divine-body destination are narrated; her remembrance does not establish identity with the Rāma born in the next chapter.

narrative_events.details: After much time Budha visits sage Kalabha’s house while the sage bathes, seizes his beautiful wife by the hair, embraces, kisses and rapes her. Sulabhā says her parents’ given name has made her easy to him, condemns the assault in her husband’s absence and curses him to become a leper in another birth whose very name people will avoid. He flees frightened to the prostitute but resumes drink and pleasure. Brahmā declines further wrongdoings, saying telling others’ faults diminishes merit. Budha eventually dies; Yama orders messengers to throw him into hell until the elemental dissolution. Having endured that, he is born in a Vaiśya home, severely leprous through the sage’s wife’s curse. The discourse condemns his deeds, prescribes clothed bathing after touching him and avoidance of his name, and says removing him will raise the craft.
narrative_events.outcome: The curse specifies a later birth; actual hell and Vaiśya-leper rebirth are narrated, ending the past-life explanation before the king requests mercy.

narrative_events.details: Hearing the messengers’ account, Śūrasena trembles, says he did not know these acts, rises and bows anxiously. He asks compassionately for a way to remove all the wrongdoer’s defects. They tell him to rise and listen: Gaṇeśa has a famous FOUR-syllable name; japa it into the man’s ear and all faults will cease like darkness at sunrise. They say he is not qualified for other remedies, so the name alone should be japped.
narrative_events.outcome: The king seeks restoration, and the servants prescribe an auditory name remedy with an explicit limitation.

narrative_events.details: At the messengers’ direction Śūrasena japs the four-syllable name into the Vaiśya’s ear THREE times, with jayapūrvam prefix wording retained. Merely hearing Gajānana, the man gains a divine body shining like the dawn sun. All sin ends through hearing the name alone; he boards the craft. By Vighnarāja’s command, the messengers immediately bring that vehicle with all its beings to Vaināyaka’s abode. Brahmā closes the answers and praises Sankaṣṭa-caturthī as righteous, fame- and life-giving, granting accomplishment by hearing, quelling suffering and obstacles, and the power of dūrvā and the name.
narrative_events.outcome: Actual hearing removes sin, gives divine body and permits collective final transport; the previously proposed exclusion is not enacted.
